lawyer:
Tufailur Rahman with Israt Jahan, Advocates—For the Petitioner. 
Kazi Mozammelul Huq, Advocate—For Respondent No. 2
parties:
Star Jute Mills Ltd ----- Petitioner
vs. 
Chairman, Divisional Labour Court ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
MM Hossain J : This Rule was issued at the instance of the petitioner calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 18-1-2001 passed by the respondent No.1 in Case No. C-40 of 1997 contained in Annexure-C should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 3. The present respondent No. 2, as the petitioner, filed a complaint case being Case No. C-40 of 1997 in the Divisional Labour Court, Khulna impleading the petitioner as opposite, party contending, inter alia, that he was appointed as clerk on 1-1-1969 in the petitioner's Mill. Being satisfied with his honesty, sincerity, efficiency and faithfulness the petitioner's Mill promoted the respondent No. 2 to the post of Accounts Assistant and thereafter, as Assistant Accounts Officer by the petitioner. During 1994-95, the respondent No. 2 performed his duties in different Jute Purchasing Centres as Accounts Officer-in-Charge. In the Jute season of 1994-95, the respondent No. 2 served as the Assistant Accounts Officer in the Charmuguria Jute Purchasing Centre. 

 4. The respondent No.2 claimed that he is a worker not having any managerial or administrative power. Two charges were brought against the respondent No. 2 containing allegations of misappropriation of money of Charmuguria Jute Purchasing Centre and certain other irregularities. He replied to the said charges in writing. The petitioner, not having been satisfied with the reply of the respondent No. 2, constituted Enquiry Committee to enquire into the charges and submit its report. The Enquiry Committee was not neutral and the respondent No. 2 was not given any opportunity to defend himself. It is stated that the respondent No. 2 was illegally dismissed from service on the basis of the enquiry report though charges were not proved against him. The said dismissal order was illegal and without lawful authority. Thereafter, the respondent No. 2, on receipt of the dismissal order on 15-7-1997, sent grievance petition on 25-7-1997 by registered post to the petitioner. As the said grievance was not redressed by the petitioner, the respondent No. 2 filed the case against the order of dismissal with a prayer for reinstatement in service with back wages by setting aside the order of dismissal. 

 5. The petitioner contested the case by filing written statement denying the material allegations stating, inter alia, that the respondent No. 2 was an Officer of the Mill and the case of the respondent No. 2 was not maintain-able under section 25(1)(b) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965. The respondent No. 2 used to exercise all managerial and supervisory powers while discharging his duties as Accounts Officer-in-Charge of Charmuguria Jute Purchasing Centre and, as such, he is not entitled to get the relief as prayed for. The petitioner is a Nationalised Jute Mill under the administrative control of Bangladesh Jute Mills Corporation. The petitioner set up jute purchasing centers at different places for purchase of raw jute. While the respondent No. 2 was employed as Assistant Accounts Officer in 1995-96 jute season in Charmuguria Jute Purchase Centre, the fact of financial irregularities and misappropriation of Taka 23,46,532 came to light. The act of misappropriation was possible due to the utter negligence of duty by the respondent No. 2. Accordingly, two show cause notices were issued upon him for actively assisting the Agency-in-charge, Abdul Hakim, in the misappropriation of money, to which he replied, but they were found to be unsatisfactory. An Enquiry Committee was constituted to enquire into the charges brought against the respondent No.2, who appeared before the Enquiry Committee and adduced evidence. He was given full opportunity to defend himself. In the enquiry, the allegations against the respondent No. 2 were proved beyond doubt and accordingly, he was dismissed from service vide order dated 15-7-1997. The respondent No. 2 filed the case with baseless allegations and, as such, it is liable to be dismissed with costs. The case was heard by the respondent No.1, who, vide his judgment and order dated 18-1-2001, was pleased to allow the case on merit by setting aside the order of the dismissal of respondent No. 2 and transforming the same into an order of discharge. 

 7. The respondent No. 2 contested the Rule by filing Affidavit-in-Opposition denying the material allegations made in the writ petition stating, inter alia, that there is no allegation against him for habitual negligence or neglect of work which constitutes misconduct for which he may be dismissed from service and, as such, the Labour Court has committed no illegality in setting aside the dismissal order of the respondent No. 2 and substituting the same with an order of discharge. The impugned judgment and order passed by the respondent No. 1 is lawful and does not suffer from any illegality and, as such, the same should be upheld and the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 8. Mr Tufailur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the respondent No. 1 failed to apply his judicial mind in passing the impugned judgment and order dated 18-1-2001 and setting aside the order of dismissal of respondent No. 2 by substituting the same with an order of discharge and also directing to implement the same within 30 days from 18-1-2001 and, as such, the Rule should be made absolute. He finally, submits that since there was no material evidence before the Labour Court to decide the case, the respondent No.1 acted illegally in allowing the application under section 25(1)(b) of the Act and, as such, the impugned judgment and order should have been declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and the Rule should be made absolute. 

 11. In support of his contention Mr Huq has referred to the case of Managing Partner, Messrs Bank Line Navigation Company vs Md Golam Mostafa and another reported in 33 DLR 149 and also the case of Manager, Zeal Bangla Sugar Mills Ltd vs Chairman, First Labour Court and another, reported in 1982 BLD 57 = 34 DLR 1 and submits that the respondent No. 2, having not committed habitual neglect of work within the meaning of section 17(3)(h) of the Act, respondent No. 1 committed no illegality in passing the impugned judgment and order and setting aside the order of dismissal of the respondent No. 2 and substituting the same with an order of discharge. He also submits that during his service career, no such allegation was made against respondent No. 2 and the respondent No. 1 rightly passed the impugned judgment and order considering the aforesaid extenuating circumstances and, as such, the Rule should be discharged. 

 13. It appears that the respondent No. 2 was the Assistant Accounts Officer of the petitioner Mill. He performed his duties in Jute Purchase Centre under the Agency-in-Charge Abdul Hakim. The allegations against the respondent No. 2 is that when he was employed as the Assistant Accounts Officer in the Jute Season of 1994-95 in Clarmuguria Jute Purchasing Centre, the fact of financial irregularities of misappropriation of Taka 14,03,046 was detected. Three inquiries were held on 14-7-1996, 31-8-1996 and 16-06-1997. According to the petitioner, during the proceeding, the respondent No. 2 was given full opportunity to defend himself. The petitioner, on completion of the inquiry proceeding, by order dated 17-7-1997, dismissed the respondent No. 2 for misconduct within the meaning of section 17(3)(h) of the Bangladesh Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965. Being aggrieved by the order of dismissal dated 15-7-1997, the respondent No. 2 filed a case being No. C-40 of 1997 before the Divisional Labour Court, Khulna. The main allegations of the respondent No.2 is that in the season of 1995-96 in Charmugaria Jute Purchasing Centre, where he was working as Assistant Accounts Officer, he aided the Agency-in-Charge, Abdul Hakim, in preparation of false blank invite in the name of the supplier, Abul Kalam Azad, on 10-2-1996 for a sum of Taka 9,43,486 and another false blank invoice in the name of the suppliers Khondaker Shahabuddin and Abu Taleb Mridha. The respondent No. 1, having considered the material evidence on record and the inquiry report submitted by the petitioner, found that- 

 15. The respondent No. 1, Divisional Lab-our Court, Khulna from the material evidence on record, found that the respondent No. 2 being an employee subordinate to the Agency-in-Charge, Abdul Hakim was persuaded by him to sign in blank memos and blank invoice to promote the business of the petitioner in the competitive market. The Enquiry Officer did not find any allegations of misappropriation of the mills fund or any illegal gratification against the respondent No. 2 in the course of his duty. It appears from the impugned judgment and order that the respondent No. 2 had been an employee of the petitioner's mill since 1966 and there is no allegation of misappropriation, corruption and habitual neglect of work against him. It also appears from the impugned judgment and order that the learned Advocate for the petitioner in the trial Court frankly conceded that in the previous service record of the respondent No. 2 there was not a single incident of misconduct. The respondent No. 1 also found to the following effect: 

 "Any worker found guilty of misconduct but not dismissed under the provisions of sub-section (1) in consideration of any extenuating circumstances, may be discharged, or suspended, as a measure of punishment, without wages as well as subsistence allowance, for a period not exceeding seven days and such period may be within or in addition to the period of suspension of the worker for enquiry under sub-section (2) of section 18, if any, or he may be otherwise punished less severely". 

 18. In the instant case before us, the case of the petitioner is that the respondent No. 2 was guilty of misconduct within the meaning of section 17(3)(h), i.e. he was guilty of habitual negligence or neglect of work. In this context Mr Huq has referred to the decision reported in 33 DLR 149 where a Division Bench of this Court held that to constitute misconduct or neglect of work mentioned in section 17(3)(h) of the Act, it must be of habitual nature. 

 19. In the instant case, it appears that the allegations against respondent No. 2 is not a solitary act, rather from materials on record, it appears that he was very much in the habit of signing of blank memos and blank invoices as per direction of the Agency-in-Charge, Abdul Hakim to help in developing the business in the competitive market. We have already noticed that the respondent No. 1, Divisional Labour Court, Khulna observed that under the direction of Agency-in-charge Abdul Hakim, the respondent No. 2 was compelled to do the same on good faith, though the act of signing of blank bill and blank advice is not permissible under the law. The respondent No. 1 also noticed that the Enquiry Officer could not find mens rea in putting his signature in blank memos and blank invoice, but no reasonable man can expect of any employee to put his signature in blank bill or blank invite as per direction of the superior authority. In all fairness, the respondent No. 2 should have apprised the superior Agency-in-charge about the consequence of such exercise which was not permissible in law. In the instant case, signing of blank memos and blank advice is definitely an act of misconduct within the meaning of section 17(3)(b) of the Act. 

 20. From the enquiry report and the impugned judgment and order, it appears that the respondent No. 2 had been in the service of the petitioner mill for more than 25 years without having any allegations of corruption or any other misconduct within the meaning of the Act of 1965. The respondent No. 1 also found that the previous record of service of the respondent No. 2 is free from allegations of corruption. 

 21. Section 18(6) of the aforesaid Act provides that in awarding punishment under this Act the employer shall take into account the gravity of the misconduct, the previous record, if any, of the worker and any other extenuating and aggravating circumstance that may exist. 

 22. In the case of Manager, Zeal Bangla Sugar Mills Ltd vs Chairman, 1st Labour Court and another reported in 1982 BLD 57 = 34 DLR 1, it has been held that the management while dismissing the delinquent worker did not take into account the extenuating circumstances that he was the first offender during his service for over 10 years, that being so, delinquent respondent shall be deemed to have been discharged under section 17(2) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965. In the instant case before us, the respondent No. 2 had been in the employment of petitioner Mill for more than 25 years without having any previous bad record of service and that in order to compete with the business of other Mill owners and for meeting the urgent demand of the petitioner Mill in developing its business and also to meet the annual sales target, the respondent No. 2 was pressed by his superior officer to put his signature in blank bills and blank advice for the betterment of the petitioner Mill. This aspect, according to our views, is an extenuating circumstance within the meaning of section 17(2) of the aforesaid Act. Accordingly, we are of the view that the Divisional Labour Court, respondent No. 1, having considered the extenuating circumstances rightly passed the impugned judgment and order in setting aside the order of dismissal of respondent No. 2 and passing an order of discharge and directing the petitioner to implement the same within 30 days from 18-1-2001. 

 23. In the case of Bank of Credit and Commerce (Overseas) Limited, now Eastern Bank Limited vs Tajul Islam Chowdhury and another reported in 45 DLR (AD) 61, it has been held that Labour Court has the power to convert an order of dismissal into one of termination of service in appropriate circumstances. 

 24. In the instant case, admittedly the respondent No. 2 has himself not misappropriated any fund of the petitioner Mill and though he has committed an act of misconduct by complying with the unlawful order of his superior officer to compete with the competitors. His previous service record has been found to be satisfactory. So, in awarding punishment under this Act, it is within discretion of the employer to consider the gravity of the misconduct, the previous record and also any other extenuating circumstance that may exist. Relying on the decision reported in 45 DLR (AD) 61 we are of the view that the respondent No. 1, Divisional Labour Court, Khulna rightly passed the impugned judgment and order dated 18-1-2001 converting the order of dismissal into an order of discharge and, as such, no interference is called for by this Hon'ble Court. We do not find any merit in this Rule. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. 

 The impugned judgment and order passed by the Divisional Labour Court, Khulna in Case No. C-40 of 1997 is declared to have been passed in accordance with law.
